title: Infrastructure and Facilities Meeting
overview: The Wausau Infrastructure and Facilities Committee met on October 8, 2026, taking several significant actions including approving an amendment to the city's winter street maintenance policy to allow snowplow counterflow to traffic on center median boulevard streets — a change sought by southeast side and Highland Park residents for three years. The committee also set 2027 construction assessment rates, approved two alley/road vacations, approved a painted curb extension project downtown, and reviewed ongoing 2026 construction projects.

discussions.item: Winter Street Maintenance Policy — Counterflow Plowing on Center Median Boulevard Streets
discussions.body: After extensive public comment from roughly ten speakers over several months of meetings, Alder Slonsky moved to amend the Department of Public Works winter maintenance policy to permit snowplow counterflow to traffic whenever otherwise safe to do so; the motion passed unanimously. City Attorney Ann Jacobson confirmed Wisconsin Statute 346.05(2) allows vehicles engaged in highway maintenance to operate on the left-hand side of the road, and that a written internal policy would protect plow drivers under city liability. DPW Director Dustin [last name inaudible] acknowledged the counterflow practice had been discontinued based on a misinterpretation — originally prompted by a state patrol comment about one-way streets that was incorrectly applied to divided two-way boulevard streets. Alder Slonsky criticized DPW for not providing requested cost/time comparisons between plowing methods as asked at the prior meeting, while Alder Martins and others praised community advocates for their thorough, data-driven advocacy over three years. District 1 Alder Carol Lukans appeared as a public commenter urging the committee to act that night so residents would not face another winter under the old policy.

City engineering staff presented proposed 2027 assessment rates, noting that at $55 per accessible foot the city recovers roughly 22% of roadway reconstruction costs — down from a historical target of 60%. Staff recommended raising the sewer lateral replacement assessment from $500 (unchanged for approximately 25 years) to $1,000, noting actual city costs range from $1,500 to $2,500 per lateral. Alder Martins moved to approve the rates with street reconstruction raised to $60 per accessible foot and the sewer lateral assessment raised to $1,000; the motion passed unanimously. Alders Heni and Slonsky raised questions about whether percentage-based assessments would be fairer than flat dollar rates, but staff explained that flat rates are required for statutory notice purposes and provide more equity across projects of varying complexity.

discussions.item: Vacating Alley Bounded by Lake View Drive, Bertha Street, Elmwood Boulevard, and Midway Boulevard
discussions.body: A motion was made and seconded to vacate the alley; city engineering noted a sanitary sewer runs through the alley and the city must retain an easement. A friendly amendment was adopted to include easement retention language, and the motion passed unanimously. Public commenter Michael Moran (2513 Elmwood Boulevard) spoke in support of the vacation during public comment.

discussions.item: Vacating 134-Foot Southerly Extension of Liberty Ridge Way
discussions.body: A speaker at the public hearing representing property owners Chris and Margaret [Gdori, phonetic] testified in support, explaining the owners want to secure the end of the road as a private drive. City engineering confirmed both sewer and water infrastructure are present and easements must be retained. Alder Heni moved to vacate with easement language; Alder Slonsky seconded after confirming engineering had no objection. A committee member asked for clarification that the remainder of Liberty Ridge Way remains a public road, which staff confirmed. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Painted Curb Extension Project — Fourth Street and Scott Street (Wausau River District)
discussions.body: TJ [last name not stated] from city staff presented a River District proposal to install plastic bollards and road paint at the east side of the Fourth and Scott intersection downtown to create pedestrian refuge areas and shorten crossing distances. The project had already been approved by the Bike and Pedestrian Committee. The River District committed in writing to cover bollard replacement costs through 2032; the Center for Visual Arts provided verbal assurance of low- or no-cost repainting assistance. Alder Slonsky moved to approve; Alder Martins seconded and expressed strong support, noting it was a proven traffic-calming method at a difficult intersection. The motion passed unanimously. Alder Wizkowski suggested exploring additional painted intersection treatments downtown, with staff noting that could be brought to a joint Bike Ped and Arts Commission meeting.

Alder Heni raised concerns about the sustainability of current borrowing levels, noting the levy is rising again, and said he is working with Director Linman to identify capital projects that could be deferred to reduce borrowing by $4–5 million. Alder Martins noted that the drinking water treatment facility solar array (projected at $1.98 million) effectively failed after a U.S. EPA grant was not received, and that a downtown street traffic flow redesign at $150,000 is still under discussion tied to TID 12. Staff emphasized that deferring road reconstruction has ripple effects pushing all subsequent projects back and frustrating residents expecting scheduled work.

Staff reported that the downtown utility project (Second Street and Division Street), Grant Street utility upgrades, and Stark Street reconstruction (5th to 12th) are all 100% complete. Eighth Avenue reconstruction (Bridge to Spruce) is approximately 90% complete with final paving expected the week of October 19th. Asphalt overlays and sidewalk projects are complete city-wide. The riverfront parking lot near Athletic Park is under construction with paving expected the following week. Staff noted this is one of the earliest project completion years in recent memory. Discussion touched on coordination challenges with the lead service line replacement contractor, and committee members advocated for better public-facing communication tools — including a simpler website flowchart and use of the existing pothole hotline (715-261-6960) and Wausau Streets email — to reduce resident confusion about road work timelines.

title: Finance Committee Budget Session #3
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee held its third budget session for the 2027 budget, covering special revenue funds, capital projects, TID districts, debt service, and enterprise funds. A significant portion of the meeting focused on the city's growing debt burden, with Alderperson Hani presenting eight budget proposals including capping borrowing, finding $4.2-5.2 million in deferrable capital projects, cutting the city administrator position, and requesting a 1% general fund reduction. The committee agreed not to meet Thursday as planned, instead giving time for members to submit written amendments for a future meeting.

discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne presented the special revenue funds including community development block grant, economic development, environmental cleanup, room tax, recycling, animal control, hazmat, and the 400 Block Riverlife fund. She noted the environmental cleanup fund reserves are declining now that an insurance annuity from the Holtz Kroy settlement has ended, and costs from EPA oversight — including a $121,000 bill last year — will eventually return to the levy. She also suggested consolidating some special revenue funds into the general fund to build up the expenditure restraint base, noting the city receives over $1 million in expenditure restraint grant funding.

Engineering staff walked through 2027 infrastructure projects including Ethel Street reconstruction, 11th Avenue, 17th Avenue STP Urban design, asphalt overlay (proposed increase from $600,000 to $800,000), lead service line replacement, and sidewalk repair. Alderperson Hani raised concern about borrowing for basic infrastructure and asked whether projects like Ethel Street could be deferred to 2028; engineering staff explained deferral simply shifts the entire street reconstruction schedule back a year and increases ongoing maintenance costs. A committee member questioned why the city pays for alley paving excavation costs while residents are assessed only for asphalt, prompting discussion about revisiting that policy.

Economic Development Manager Patrick presented TID 8 (MBX South demolition and environmental cleanup, with a $250,000 WEDC brownfield grant applied for), TID 11 (business campus site prep and marketing for a large development site off Innovation Way), and TID 12 (limited expenditures due to ongoing deficits, projected to remain in deficit for approximately 10 years). Jefferson parking ramp HVAC replacement was identified as a critical project after one of two redundant systems failed. The former Sears ramp east wall — exposed after the Sears building demolition — needs $700,000 in waterproofing and rehabilitation. A Forest Street engineering and planning project of $150,000 was discussed as enabling future LRIP and STP Urban grant applications.

Maryanne presented a detailed debt analysis showing the city's outstanding general obligation debt at approximately 33.38% of equalized value (limit is 5%), projected to rise to 33.81% after proposed 2027 borrowing. She compared the 2016 infrastructure borrowing of $2.8 million at 1.54% interest (resulting in a $338,000 annual payment) to the proposed 2027 borrowing of $6.2 million estimated at approximately 4.27% (resulting in roughly $770,000 annually plus $216,000 for the lead service line loan). She proposed using TID 8's approximately $11 million in remaining increment capacity to absorb roughly $2.18 million in infrastructure costs, reducing the levy impact by approximately $275,000 annually. She also suggested a 10-year plan to incrementally add $130,000 per year to levy-funded capital to eventually take asphalt overlay and concrete repairs off debt.

discussions.item: Enterprise Funds: Metro Ride, Airport, Parking
discussions.body: The committee discussed that Metro Ride and the municipal airport operate at deficits covered by the general fund. Alderperson Hani raised constituent concerns about deficit operations, while Alderperson Tierney noted some municipal services like transit are inherently not self-sustaining but enhance quality of life. It was explained that Metro Ride cannot expand service to surrounding municipalities like Rib Mountain because those communities have not invited the city in and would need to help subsidize service, as Wisconsin does not permit regional transit authorities. New Metro Ride buses are coming through the Volkswagen emissions settlement. Airport revenue discussion included land lease payments, property taxes on privately-owned hangars, and past fuel-flow surcharge revenue that was discontinued when aviation fuel prices rose.

Engineering Director Eric provided an overview of a storm water utility concept at committee request, explaining that currently 65% of storm water costs are borne by residential taxpayers rather than major impervious-surface users such as large parking lots and commercial buildings. A storm water utility would distribute costs based on equivalent dwelling units tied to impervious surface area, bringing in non-taxable entities like nonprofits as payers, with a corresponding reduction in the levy. Maryanne noted a consultant study funded by a grant is completed and a presentation is scheduled for the October 27th city council meeting.

discussions.item: Alderperson Hani's Budget Proposals and Next Steps
discussions.body: Alderperson Hani presented eight budget proposals including: capping 2027 borrowing at $17-18 million or reducing debt by $1 million; identifying $4.2-5.2 million in deferrable capital projects; a 1% general fund spending reduction; removing $150,000 for the city administrator position; a motorpool charge reconciliation; a current accounting of committed versus unassigned general fund balance; asking the mayor to direct Metro Ride, airport, and parking to develop 5-year financial plans; a reconciled capital project schedule; and a 5-year debt forecast separated by general government, water, and wastewater. The committee agreed not to meet Thursday, directing members to submit written amendments to Maryanne, who will distribute them and incorporate approved changes as a budget insert. Alder Watson was noted as also having proposals to submit.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Resident Water Quality Complaint
discussions.body: Resident Lori Foundry of Rainbow Drive/County Road XX described severe black and orange sludge in her water supply, corroded fixtures, clogged drains, and water she considers unsafe to drink or use for washing food. Greg (Public Works Director) explained the problem stems from manganese buildup at a dead-end line serving only two customers, and that flushing every six to eight weeks has not resolved the issue. The committee discussed options including pipe scrubbing, installing an RO filtration system, exploring a pipe-looping project estimated at $300,000–$400,000, and potentially obtaining an easement from a neighboring property. Staff committed to having lead water utility worker Mark Mackey visit the property to take water samples, and the committee expressed willingness to provide some form of bill compensation. The looping project was identified as a candidate for the Capital Improvement Plan.
Jim Buck moved and Jessica Stowell seconded to approve the June committee meeting minutes. No discussion was noted. The motion carried unanimously 4-0 on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Director of Public Works and Utilities Report - Lift Station No. 3
discussions.body: Greg reported that wipes are clogging the vacuum-style Lift Station No. 3 nearly every day, requiring staff to spend roughly 1.5 hours daily clearing pumps at significant cost. Letters were mailed to customers warning against flushing wipes. The committee discussed using sewer cameras to identify offending addresses once a new utility employee starts the following Monday, and confirmed the village ordinance allows billing customers for damages caused by illegal dumping. Greg noted plans to televise sewer lines and work with Green Bay Pipe and TV to pinpoint problem sources.

discussions.item: Director of Public Works and Utilities Report - Village Garage Project
discussions.body: Greg reported that the public works crew completed site excavation and gravel base work for the village garage project, and that ST Ellenbecker is expected to begin pouring concrete imminently, before cold weather requires heat blankets.

discussions.item: Finance and Treasurer Report - August Financial Statements
discussions.body: John (Finance/Treasurer) reported that the water utility showed revenues of approximately $513,000 through eight months against a positive fund balance of $183,000 after expenses, slightly below the prior year's $217,000 surplus. The sewer utility showed revenues of $786,000 against a surplus of $198,000, lower than the prior year's $312,000 due to elevated Rib Mountain Metro Sewage District charges that surged from a budgeted $460,000 to an estimated $572,000 for 2026. Total water utility debt stands at approximately $2.949 million, scheduled for payoff in 2043; the sewer utility currently carries no debt. No rate increases are anticipated for 2027.

discussions.item: Septic Tank Ordinance Discussion - Northland Lutheran High School Holding Tank Request
discussions.body: A representative from Northland Lutheran High School presented the school's request to install a holding tank for a small concession stand with two single-stall bathrooms used seasonally for soccer and baseball games, located approximately 407 feet from the nearest utility lateral. The committee developed amended ordinance language including: non-residential use only, seasonal use up to seven months, minimum 400 feet from nearest lateral, minimum lot size of one acre, tank size meeting Marathon County minimum requirements, and requiring approval from both the Public Works Director and the Utility Committee. Jim Buck moved and Dan Raskowski seconded to recommend the amended ordinance change to the Plan Commission and Village Board; the motion carried 4-0. Staff will draft language and consult the village attorney on whether a public hearing is required.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Discussion - Water and Sewer Utilities
discussions.body: John and Greg presented the proposed 2027 utility budgets. No water or sewer rate increases are proposed for 2027. On the sewer side, projected revenues of approximately $1.371 million and inclusion of $548,100 in Rib Mountain Metro costs still yield a projected net profit of roughly $7,800, making a rate increase unnecessary. On the water side, revenues are projected at $947,000 driven in part by an estimated $90,000 in connection fees from the Marathon County garage project; after accounting for expenses including one additional half-time crew employee shared between water and sewer, the water utility is near break-even. The committee also discussed the Marathon County garage's plans to use wells for brine-making and car wash operations rather than municipal water, with committee member Alex Fedbeck pushing for a cost-benefit analysis on requiring municipal water connection to capture long-term revenue. Borrowing for the 2027–2029 CIP is proposed to be delayed until after July 1, 2027, to defer principal and interest costs to the 2028 budget.

title: Finance Committee Budget Session #2
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee held its second budget session for the 2027 budget, hearing presentations from the police, fire, transit, and general government departments. The session was dominated by a lengthy debate over Flock automated license plate recognition cameras, with several alderpersons expressing concern about civil liberties and data privacy while Police Chief defended the technology and its contractual obligations through 2028. No formal votes were taken during this session; budget amendments were held for later consolidation.

discussions.body: Police Chief presented a largely cost-to-continue budget with targeted savings totaling approximately $150,000, including: eliminating the contract with All City Management Services for crossing guards (saving ~$40,000–$45,000), cutting the CSO budget by roughly half (~$45,000), reducing the non-dog animal control (cat contract) budget from $37,000 to $18,500, and pursuing a renegotiated school resource officer contract with the school district at 100% district-funded cost for the school year (projected new revenue of $56,000). The department will also reduce sworn positions from 81 to 80 following expiration of Jed Alexander Foundation funding for downtown beat officers, while repurposing a patrol officer to continue the two-officer downtown program.

Alder Tom Neil called for removing the $50,000 Flock camera line item from the budget, citing concerns about corporate data practices and residents' distrust of the company. Alder Hani echoed concerns about Fourth Amendment implications and the potential for abuse of dragnet surveillance, though both alderpersons stated they trusted the current department leadership. The Police Chief defended Flock vigorously, stating the city's contract runs through December 31, 2028 with no exit-for-convenience clause, that data is city-owned and cannot be sold to third parties, that images are deleted after 30 days, and that exiting the contract could expose the city to financial liability. Mayor Doug Diny supported keeping the cameras, noting Wausau's policy is among the best in the state. Alder Tierney requested the department's written Flock policy be shared with all council members. The Police Chief noted a second public presentation to the Public Health and Safety Committee is scheduled for October 19th.

Alder Watson proposed a budget amendment to reduce the 2027 pet license fee for spayed/neutered dogs or cats to $25 (from $30), with a $10 microchip discount, and fund any resulting revenue shortfall from the animal control fund balance of approximately $146,000. Finance Director Maryanne clarified that the fund balance is separate from approximately $41,954 held in a liability account owed to the county. Watson expressed intent to use the coming year to gather data on the program and have a deeper policy discussion about whether animal control should be partially levy-supported rather than fully user-fee funded. The amendment was tabled for later consolidation with other budget amendments.

Fire Deputy Chief presented a budget relying on modest cuts across multiple line items — including eliminating the FDIC national conference travel, cutting psychological services, reducing software subscriptions, and proposing to purchase a robotic mower (~$10,000 savings) to eliminate the mowing contract at Station 2. The operations division chief position will remain vacant through July 1, 2027, and a retiring 40-hour employee's position will also be left open for six months to meet budget targets. The Chief noted the department is currently down six members from full staff and that overtime is a growing concern. A presentation on making the community care paramedic position permanent is forthcoming to the HR and Finance committees, with Aspirus verbally committing to continue funding support after the three-year trial ends in 2027.

Transit Director Ron (approximately six months in the role) presented a budget reduced by $81,635 through historical spending analysis and adjustments. Key drivers of savings include 10 new buses replacing 2009-era vehicles, which will dramatically reduce fuel and maintenance costs as most of the fleet will be under warranty. The CAD AVL system cost increase will be fully covered by FTA ARPA funds through 2028, but will create a significant budget increase after 2029. A forthcoming UMO Wisco fare payment system, not yet before the council, would add operating costs but is projected to increase ridership. The FTA's indirect cost reimbursement rate increased from 10% to 15%, generating roughly $500,000 in general fund revenue that offsets the transit levy.

The city attorney's office and other general government departments presented small budgets with limited flexibility, primarily consisting of personnel, dues, licensing fees, and court-related costs. One assistant position in the city attorney's office remains frozen and unfilled. The office noted it recently left Westlaw, its online legal subscription service, as a cost-saving measure. Specific dollar amounts for general government savings were not detailed in the portion of the transcript captured.

discussions.item: 4A: 1300 Cleveland Avenue - EPA Technical Assistance and Deed Restriction
discussions.body: Staff reported the city has been confirmed eligible for EPA technical assistance, which would provide a consultant to conduct a financial feasibility analysis of reuse options identified through public engagement. Alder Kilian expressed concern that an email sent to the EPA by city staff characterized the public-identified reuse options as 'too narrow,' saying the committee and residents had never been told that. Kilian also raised that the property continues to be used for industrial purposes—including storage of trailers, old lampposts, and vehicles by DPW and the fire department—which she said undermined resident trust. City Attorney Jacobson confirmed it is legally permissible to place a deed restriction on city-owned property but noted the zoning has already been changed to residential and that any future council could remove a deed restriction. The committee debated how specific the restriction should be, with Alder Neil cautioning against language so narrow it might deter beneficial development. The committee ultimately directed staff and the city attorney, with input from Alder Kilian, to draft a deed restriction prohibiting industrial use consistent with public input meeting outcomes, to be brought back for formal approval at the next meeting. Staff also noted a 2024 council resolution allows limited DPW training use of the site, which may need to be revisited.

discussions.body: Director Fick explained the planning and due diligence agreement would give the city exclusive access to the county-owned UWSP campus property for six months to conduct architectural, engineering, and environmental review, contingent on a budget modification for the fire and police departments also passing at the next council meeting. Alder Neil noted a prior council vote on feasibility funding had failed but that the item was reintroduced after the required 30-day waiting period and would come before council the following Tuesday. discussions.item: Rib Mountain Law Enforcement Services Contract Update
discussions.body: County Administrator Leonard reported that negotiations with Rib Mountain are ongoing and productive, with a follow-up meeting scheduled the following week involving the sheriff and Rib Mountain representatives. discussions.item: WDNR Final Decision on Corrosion Control Treatment (Ortho Phosphate)
discussions.body: Staff (identified as Eric and Scott) briefed the commission that the DNR issued a final decision in July requiring ortho phosphate to be operational no later than July 9, 2028. Staff noted a plan to install a temporary feed system before the permanent system is bid out in early 2027 to allow pipes to season ahead of required sampling. A commission member (Martins) asked whether progress on lead service line replacement could reduce or delay the ortho phosphate requirement; staff clarified it also benefits copper and in-home fixtures, so the requirement stands regardless. discussions.body: Ben reported that the wastewater headworks project is nearing substantial completion with an October 15 deadline expected to be met; a programming issue by Hydrodyne was resolved. discussions.body: Staff presented a spreadsheet of proposed capital projects highlighted for potential PFAS settlement funding use over the next five years, including the ortho phosphate installation, noting $1.67 million in EPA funding already secured with a remaining shortfall proposed to be covered by settlement funds rather than borrowing. Staff acknowledged the spreadsheet totals are not accurate and promised a corrected version for November. title: Community Life, Infrastructure and Public Property (CLIPP) Committee Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter CLIPP Committee held its second review of the proposed 2027-2036 Capital Improvement Program (CIP), a 10-year plan totaling approximately $4.3 million in 2027 expenditures across roads, parks, utilities, public safety equipment, and facilities. No formal vote was taken on the CIP itself, as adoption is scheduled for the November 9 budget hearing; discussion focused on project priorities including Maple Ridge Road reconstruction, fire truck preordering timelines, lift station upgrades, a future water tower and well, and parks improvements at Bushga Park. The committee also briefly addressed a $1.2 million borrowing deadline of October 2027 and the fiscal implications of shifting $863,000 in TID 2 proceeds back to the village's general debt service.

discussions.body: Village Administrator John presented the second draft of the 10-year CIP, noting the primary additions since the first draft were park committee items with cost estimates placed into specific years. He emphasized the 2027 year is the only year being formally adopted in the upcoming budget cycle, with 2028-2036 serving as a planning tool. The total proposed 2027 CIP expenditure is approximately $4.3 million spread across the general fund, capital projects fund, capital equipment fund, utility funds, and the park improvement fund. The administrator stressed the village has historically failed to invest in infrastructure — one employee noted it had been 26 years since the village last paved a road.

The administrator noted the rescue/fire truck slotted for 2029 requires a formal commitment to preorder three to four years in advance, meaning an order placed now would likely not be received until 2030 or later. No down payment is required at order time, but the village board would need to sign a preorder agreement in a future budget year. The committee acknowledged this commitment does not need to be finalized in the next few months but cannot be deferred indefinitely without pushing delivery further out.

Trustee Myszka and President Joling identified Maple Ridge Road as the highest priority road project, noting it is the only village road with freeway access and the county recently improved adjacent county roads. Public Works Director Greg confirmed that core samples have been taken but a full engineering design is still needed; realistically, construction would begin in 2028 at the earliest. The administrator proposed potentially splitting the project across 2027 (engineering/design) and 2028 (construction), and noted that $1.2 million in leftover 2024 borrowing proceeds — which must be spent by October 2027 — could be committed to Maple Ridge. The committee discussed that approved bids from the village board may be sufficient to legally 'commit' those funds by the deadline. A question was raised about whether the steep hill section east of Spring could be graded down; Greg cautioned this would involve significant excavation costs, slope design, and potential DNR involvement.

Trustee [Patty Tukowski] raised concerns that only modest capital funds were set aside in 2027 for the municipal building despite known maintenance issues including roof leaks. The administrator acknowledged the building has suffered from years of inconsistent maintenance and explained that some repairs — such as heated roof tape and handicap entrance fixes — would be absorbed into the operational budget rather than the capital plan. He framed the CIP as a working document that will evolve as priorities shift.

discussions.item: Parks CIP Items and Fundraising Update
discussions.body: The parks committee additions, including playground equipment for Bushga Park and fencing for other parks, were incorporated into the CIP with 2027 borrowing projected at approximately $175,000, partially offset by $25,000 from the park improvement fund. Trustee [Patty Tukowski] noted the parks committee had unanimously recommended adding a zip line and rubber surface to Friendship Park for the 2029 improvement cycle; the administrator acknowledged this was not yet in the document and committed to adding it before the October 19-20 budget workshops. On fundraising, Trustee Myszka reported approximately $20,000 raised to date, including $1,348 from the 5K event and a $236 donation from the 50/50 raffle winner.

discussions.item: Sewer and Water Utility CIP Items
discussions.body: Public Works Director Greg detailed planned lift station upgrades (stations 5, 7, 9 panel replacements and generator additions), the removal of lift station 10 serving approximately 60 homes, and the in-progress removal of lift station 3 which uses a vacuum system prone to daily clogging. He highlighted the need for a vac/jet back truck (approximately $500,000) and a waste truck, both of which are dependent on the new garage being completed around February. The water utility section flagged a projected $11 million need for a new well and water tower, with the administrator cautioning this is a rough high estimate spread over multiple years and subject to a five-to-six-year Public Service Commission approval process. A potential TIF district was discussed as a way to offset water infrastructure costs, though TID 1 in the target area is severely distressed and cannot be overlaid with a new TID boundary.

The administrator explained that shifting $863,000 in TID 2 bond proceeds back to the village's general debt service — because the Flanner Jamerals project came in over budget and did not use those proceeds — will modestly increase the village's tax levy debt service obligation but allow TID 2 to close earlier, potentially releasing approximately $80 million in valuation and generating an estimated $250,000 annually in additional property tax revenue. Trustee [Paul Maja] recalled the administrator's earlier explanation that a significant drop in existing debt service around 2029 would help absorb new borrowing, which the administrator confirmed but noted the restructuring has reduced two prior projected drops to one drop of approximately $200,000 in 2029. For 2027, general obligation borrowing is proposed for only two projects: Bushga Park playground equipment and Maple Ridge Road, totaling approximately $1.8 million.

The administrator noted that completing Kronenwetter Drive in 2025 ($2.2 million project) has already increased the village's annual state highway aid by over $50,000 for the 2027 budget year due to the state's three-year and six-year spending averages. He projected that continuing capital investments in roads and police staffing would further increase highway aid in 2028 and beyond, framing infrastructure investment as self-reinforcing from a revenue standpoint.

Trustee [Patty Tukowski] indicated she would be working the election and would need to start at 6:30 a.m.; the committee briefly discussed moving the meeting start time to 5:30 p.m. with general agreement but no formal action. discussions.body: Jamie presented a county-owned parcel on 28th Avenue, originally purchased in 2006 for a highway corridor that was never built, now offered to the city. discussions.item: 5A: Hearing – Appeal of Tree Assessment Fee, 4011 Stone Ridge Drive
discussions.body: The committee conducted a formal quasi-judicial hearing on homeowner Jonathan Mafam's appeal of a city forester fee for damaging a city tree during unpermitted excavation. City plumbing inspector Dennis Keski testified that he found trenching had been done without an excavation or lateral permit and that as of the morning of the meeting no permit had been obtained. City forester John Kahan, a board-certified master arborist, testified the tree was losing leaves early due to root damage caused by the trenching, that the permit process would have identified a safer route or offered tree removal for a $550 fee, and that a pre-existing seam/occlusion in the tree was unrelated to the dieback. Mafam testified he purchased the home in September 2024, suffered a flooded finished basement and $30,000 in losses in the first spring, and was trying to install a French drain system; he stated he did not know he needed a permit, did not know the tree was a city tree, his contractor abandoned the job incomplete, and he was asking for leniency. He disputed John's characterization of his visit to the property. After testimony and committee questions, Alder Slonsky moved to adjourn into closed session for deliberation; the motion passed on a 4-0 roll call vote.

title: Finance Committee Budget Session #1
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee held its first of four budget workshop sessions for the 2027 city budget on October 5, 2026. The proposed budget includes a total city levy of $40.63 million, up $2.5 million (6.76%) from the prior year, with $1.45 million of the increase driven by a voter-approved referendum. The session covered high-level budget impacts, public works, motorpool, water/wastewater, and parks department budgets, with significant discussion around motorpool funding shortfalls, health insurance cost pressures, and the need for revenue diversification.

discussions.body: Mayor Doug Diny presented the top-line 2027 budget: $40.63 million total city levy, up $2.5 million from 2026, with an assessed tax rate of $9.24 per thousand. He noted that $1.45 million of the increase (3.8%) is attributable to the voter-approved referendum, and the remaining 1.9% stems from operational factors. Directors were directed to seek a 2% decrease in cost-to-continue expenses; four positions are being held vacant (~$410,000 in savings). A new city administrator position at $150,000 is included, envisioned to review and implement recommendations from a pending citywide audit. No new fees are proposed, consistent with the council's stated opposition to regressive fees.

discussions.item: Finance Director Budget Presentation — Revenues, Levy, and Assessed Value
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne detailed that computer aid came in at $557,000 versus a budgeted $513,000, yielding approximately $44,000 in additional revenue — a modification not yet reflected in the budget book. She noted assessed value is estimated at 1% growth pending mid-October confirmation, meaning the tax rate could shift. Impact on a median home is estimated at $99.73. She also distributed a Forward Analytics report showing Marathon County's net new construction is covering only about half of CPI growth since 2010, illustrating structural revenue constraints. The garbage contract increase of approximately $291,000 — absorbed into the levy rather than passed to ratepayers — was cited as a key cost pressure.

discussions.item: Position Vacancies and HR Position Authorization
discussions.body: An alderperson (identified as Vicki in context) raised a concern that an additional HR position budgeted at $100,000 had not been fully authorized by the council, noting she voted against it previously and was unaware of it returning for a vote. Maryanne and other officials explained the position is being brought back at the HR committee meeting the following week, and that it had previously been approved with the understanding it would be filled after a new director was hired. The vacancies held open include: one downtown police officer FTE (previously foundation-funded), one assistant city attorney FTE, a half-year fire division chief/inspection lieutenant FTE, a DPW surveyor half-FTE, a parks administrative coordinator half-FTE, and a CCITC project manager FTE.

DPW Director Eric presented the public works budget, which decreased roughly 4% overall. Discussion focused on leaf pickup operations — clarifying the city never conducted two full collections but eliminated the two-phase map that caused public confusion. Alderperson Watson raised a concern about significant reductions in contractual services (~$80,000) relative to the DPW request, with Eric noting the cuts were made line-by-line with the mayor and finance director and that the city surveyor position remains unfilled due to lack of qualified applicants. Fee structure was discussed, with committee members noting inspection and land-use permit fees remained flat while animal licensing fees were proposed to increase — a disparity questioned by at least one alderperson.

The motorpool discussion revealed a recurring structural shortfall: departments requiring motorpool services cannot afford full cost recovery through their levy-funded budgets. In 2025, actual motorpool charges to the general fund totaled $5.6 million against budgeted amounts of $4.1 million, leaving a $1.4 million gap partially covered by investment income ($370,000) and departmental savings. Alderperson Hanie questioned how many Mercury audit recommendations had been implemented; fleet staff confirmed four were addressed (hiring a fleet analyst, reassessing rental rates, increasing staffing, reducing fleet age) but acknowledged the core problem is that departments cannot afford the equipment they need. Eric argued the city must diversify revenue — specifically citing a wheel tax, stormwater utility, and converting garbage to a special charge — to sustainably fund motorpool. The aerial truck replacement was flagged as a deferred need: lead time is 24 months for a standard model or up to 51 months for a custom unit; a vendor offered a ~$200,000 discount for prepayment, which the city historically does not do.

Eric and Maryanne presented both utility budgets, which remained relatively flat year-over-year. discussions.item: Staff presentation: Options for county engagement with Alliant Energy
discussions.body: County Administrator Lori McSkimmons presented a table of four options for the board: (1) negotiating a Joint Developer Agreement (JDA), estimated cost up to $20,000; (2) intervening in the PSC permitting process, estimated $75,000–$200,000+; (3) adopting a moratorium, cost unknown and noted as likely unenforceable on a 100-megawatt project; and (4) appealing the PSC's decision after issuance, estimated $20,000–$50,000. She noted PSC staff confirmed no intervention has ever stopped a project and that Columbia County's similar moratorium effort was sent back to committee. She emphasized options are not mutually exclusive and that the county could not file for intervention until after Alliant submits its formal PSC application, which could come as early as mid-December 2026.

discussions.item: Resolution 55-26 — Hub City Wind Project engagement with Alliant Energy
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson, who authored the resolution and chaired the alternative energy advisory committee, explained it does not commit the county to a JDA but rather asks Alliant Energy to submit a draft proposal addressing community concerns by November 1st, after which the board would evaluate next steps. Supervisor Dickinson expressed strong opposition, stating he would not vote for anything that moved toward a JDA and questioned whether Alliant would engage in good faith. Supervisor Leur raised concerns that the resolution puts the county in a reactive position and called for an energy summit to address broader regional energy policy. Supervisor Ritter, Supervisor Nath, Supervisor Rosenberg, and Supervisor Robinson defended the resolution as a proactive first step to gauge Alliant's willingness to address constituents' concerns on issues including decommissioning, setbacks, emergency response, property values, and health impacts. The resolution passed but was noted by Chair Gibbs as not unanimous.

He highlighted continued funding for homelessness emergency shelter ($150,000), childcare workforce expansion ($50,000 reduced level), a minimum revenue guarantee for Central Wisconsin Airport ($150,000 tied to a $950,000 federal air service development grant requiring local match), and $100,000 for PC replacements. discussions.body: Community Development Director Nathan Sandwick presented the preliminary plan for approximately 60+ one-acre lots with private wells and septic systems, noting unanimous planning commission approval in June. Board discussion focused on the history of the property (turned down nine times under previous developer), the decision not to extend municipal sewer and water due to costs over $1.6 million, and the compromise of one-acre lots meeting septic minimums. Concerns were raised about traffic on Nick Avenue, which will be gated as emergency access only. Trustee Mishka moved to approve, seconded by Trustee Coyle; the motion passed 7-0.

discussions.item: Text Amendment Chapter 520 - Zero Lot Line Structures
discussions.body: Sandwick presented a zoning ordinance amendment to allow twin homes (zero-lot-line structures) where duplexes are currently permitted on 20,000 square foot parcels, enabling each half to be individually owned. Trustee Lesniak moved to approve, seconded by Trustee Stowell. No notable debate was recorded; the amendment passed 7-0 on a roll call vote.

discussions.item: Budget Preview - Garbage Fees and Debt
discussions.body: Jacobs reported a $56,000 increase in state transportation aid for the 2027 budget. On garbage fees, he presented scenarios driven by diesel fuel surcharges in the Harder's contract; with diesel exceeding $6.50/gallon, the village faces a $57,000 shortfall in 2026. The planning figure recommended by APC of $6.25/gallon would raise household garbage fees from $228 to approximately $267.24 per year (a $39 increase). Administrator Dabel recommended using $6.25 as the planning factor for the budget while monitoring prices. Jacobs also outlined a debt restructuring plan to shift $863,000 in unused TID 2 bond proceeds to the capital project fund, reducing TID 2 debt and freeing resources, with the tax levy absorbing a small $12,000 increase in annual debt service.

Jacobs presented the second review of the 10-year CIP, emphasizing only 43% of the $30 million plan relies on general obligation borrowing. For 2027, two borrowing projects are proposed: Maple Ridge Road (total ~$2.9M, with $1.2M already on hand reducing new borrowing to ~$1.7M) and Bushna Park improvements (~$25,000 from the park fund plus borrowed remainder). Board discussion touched on building security upgrades including key fob access (~$100,000 estimate) and cameras, audio-visual improvements to the meeting room, and the need for a long-range plan for municipal center maintenance. Jacobs noted the plan is a fluid document to be reviewed annually.

title: Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee
overview: The Village of Weston held a joint Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee meeting of the Village Board of Trustees and Planning Commission to review progress on a 10-year comprehensive plan update. Consultant Mark Roers of MD Roers Consulting presented survey results, stakeholder interview findings, draft vision statements, and preliminary chapter goals and initiatives covering land use, economic development, housing, transportation, and intergovernmental cooperation. The committee reached consensus on using draft vision statement 'C' for public presentation and set a public workshop for November 12, 2024, from 5 to 7 p.m.

discussions.body: No speakers appeared in person or online. An emailed written comment from resident Sarah Prather regarding an indoor playground, addressed to Jennifer Higgins, Jamie Sean, Mark Roers, and Audrey Webster, was distributed to the board. President Maloney noted it would be entered into the record and included in the packet.

Consultant Mark Roers outlined the comprehensive plan update process, noting that a community survey drew nearly 700 respondents, stakeholder interviews reached 24 identified contacts with 10 completing interviews, and a young adult questionnaire targeting ages 20–35 yielded 48 responses via social media. Roers explained the plan is divided into three volumes, with Volume 2 (Vision and Directions) as the current focus, targeting a public hearing by March. The board noted that 48 young adult responses exceeded the typical weekly newsletter poll response of about 27.

discussions.item: Stakeholder Interview and Young Adult Questionnaire Results
discussions.body: Roers summarized cross-cutting themes from all input channels: safety ranked as the top community value across all age groups; residents want more retail, restaurants, and groceries; interviewees emphasized need for workforce housing, particularly entry-level single-family homes and duplexes over large apartment complexes; and intergovernmental respondents favored expanding collaborative services while keeping Weston's suburban character distinct from larger neighbors. Young adults specifically cited school quality, parks, family orientation, housing affordability, and indoor recreation as priorities.

Roers presented three vision statement options (A from 2016, B from the recent strategic plan, and C newly drafted by Roers with AI assistance). Pre-meeting homework showed C received seven votes, A received one, and B received none. Discussion focused on tweaking C: Trustee Brent Olson suggested removing the word 'thoughtfully' from 'Weston will grow thoughtfully,' with others suggesting 'intentionally' as a substitute; one reviewer had suggested removing 'and welcoming' from the opening line, which drew pushback; another suggested adding 'can' language in multiple places, which was debated. The committee reached consensus to bring a refined version of C to the November 12 public workshop.

discussions.item: Community Growth Map and Geographic Vision
discussions.body: Roers presented a generalized growth pattern map highlighting three mixed-use corridors (Scoffield Avenue, County Road X/Camp Phillips Road, and Weston Avenue) and identified a potential third interchange at Ryan Street as a priority transportation and land use initiative. Trustee or commissioner Gary Garn noted that Marathon County has a no-trucking restriction on Highway J south of Weston Avenue, which would need to be addressed for future southern industrial expansion. Extended discussion covered a potential bridge crossing north from the Caleb Drive area of Sandy Lane subdivision to improve connectivity, with staff noting the Oakclair River floodplain narrows at that point and that the northeast annexation area is known to the town chair.

Roers recommended a draft initiative to 'support more industrial development while restricting hyperscale projects,' defining hyperscale as typically requiring 100 or more acres. He cited the DeForest example of a 1,500-acre proposal that was rejected and noted concerns about power consumption, long construction periods, land obsolescence, and community division. Board members expressed agreement with establishing a policy and raised questions about when to address related issues such as solar fields, wind turbines, and EV chargers. Roers noted solar field incentives are diminishing and cited a 2,500-acre proposal near Cambridge. The committee appeared to support the proposed policy direction without a formal vote.

discussions.item: Housing Chapter and State Law Initiatives
discussions.body: Roers outlined new state-level tools including a pay-as-you-go TIF district specifically for residential development on lots no larger than 7,500 square feet with house size caps (1,500 sq ft single-story, 2,000 sq ft two-story), aimed at starter homes. He also noted infrastructure reimbursement mechanisms for developers and referenced the Truth in Planning law requiring communities to plan for sufficient housing land and be open to rezoning consistent with their plans. The board asked whether developer-fronted infrastructure costs could deter development; Roers said hybrid approaches are possible and that lenders are generally familiar with these structures.

Roers explained that TID No. 1, the larger of Weston's two active districts, will close at year-end, creating room to establish new, smaller, project-specific TIDs. He cited DeForest's model of seven active TIDs and described the shift toward pay-as-you-go (PAYGO) structures where developers front infrastructure costs and are reimbursed through incremental tax revenue, closing districts faster. No vote was taken.

Staff reported results of a pre-meeting homework exercise in which board and commission members ranked draft initiatives. 'Continue existing and pursue more opportunities for collaborative services' ranked first with six votes. Tied for second with five votes each were 'maintain the function and condition of Weston's roads' and 'help expand and attract retailers, restaurants, grocers, and industries in targeted sectors.' Tied for third with four votes each were 'phase growth according to utility, road, stormwater, and service capacity,' 'reinvest in older neighborhoods and housing,' and 'update Weston's five-year strategic plan.'

The committee confirmed a public workshop titled 'Shaping Weston's Tomorrow' for November 12, 2024, from 5 to 7 p.m. Roers outlined plans for interactive small-group discussions rather than a lecture format, organized around topics such as transportation and natural resources. A board member requested a poster be created within 22 hours to publicize the event at a community event the following evening; staff confirmed they could produce one using Canva. Roers encouraged board members who attend to listen rather than actively participate in small groups.

A resident named Grace, of 603 Jessica Street, offered three comments: she thanked committee members for asking probing questions about the ice rink proposal at Kennedy Park; she requested a more formal, structured presentation on Kennedy Park's progress and future plans, rather than informal monthly updates; and she asked whether Prohaska Park has a sign, bathrooms, and regular mowing. Staff confirmed the park has a sign and that only the walking trails are mowed, with no formal amenity area.

Staff reported that contractors are scheduled to arrive the following week to address touch-up paint on poles, crack block and missing mortar, dugout door adjustments, sod restoration from irrigation leak repairs, and irrigation system restoration. discussions.body: Staff reported that following the September 3rd public input meeting, the consultant revised the concept design to add tennis and basketball courts and relocated the shelter near the pickleball/basketball/tennis area. Public feedback on the concept was largely positive with few suggested changes. Three emails were received requesting that any future playground addition be fully ADA-accessible. Staff noted playground equipment at Muler was intentionally excluded from the seven-playground replacement project due to its relative newness (installed 2007), but replacement would be planned if the master plan moves forward. discussions.item: Discussion and action on farmers market end-of-season survey
discussions.body: Staff presented revised survey questions for a second end-of-season farmers market survey, noting the first survey was issued too early in the season. Committee members discussed whether to include a vendor-specific survey; staff noted the existing survey already asks respondents to identify as vendors. Trustee Beck, participating online, supported conducting the survey now while the season is fresh. discussions.item: Discussion on collecting feedback regarding ice skating rinks at Kennedy Park
discussions.body: Staff recapped discussions from March and April about the cost and usage of the Kennedy Park outdoor ice rink, noting that since the warming house closed in 2019, attendance tracking has been limited but staff observe regular use. Cost to maintain the rink is primarily utilities—approximately $800 in water usage annually—since labor costs remain fixed regardless. Committee members debated whether a public survey would be useful, with concern that respondents without context might vote against a low-cost community amenity. One member noted the rink is the only full-size outdoor hockey rink (200x85 feet) in the area. The committee reached a consensus not to conduct a standalone ice rink survey, but agreed to add a question about Kennedy Park usage to the existing farmers market survey. No formal vote was taken on the ice rink item.

discussions.item: Discussion and action on completing an updated aquatic center evaluation
discussions.body: Staff noted the last aquatic center evaluation was completed in 2016 at just under $7,000, and that significant capital expenditures have followed, including over $102,000 in leak repairs this year and another motor and valve replacement project exceeding $100,000. Staff estimated a new evaluation could cost $7,000–$12,000. A committee member raised the question of whether to wait given ongoing discussions about a possible pool partnership with the Everest School District, which recently mailed a facilities survey to residents. After discussion, the committee agreed that an evaluation could actually inform the partnership decision. A motion was made and seconded to proceed with the aquatic center evaluation; the motion was approved unanimously on a voice vote.

overview: The Wausau Police & Fire Commission met on September 28, 2026, conducting organizational business including electing a new vice president and secretary after Commissioner Tom Garver's departure from the commission. The meeting featured substantive updates from Fire Deputy Chief Justin and Police Chief Barnes covering apprenticeship hiring, budget constraints, the proposed UW campus acquisition, and the department's Flock license plate recognition camera system.

discussions.body: Outgoing Commissioner Tom Garver, of 4620 Huntington Court, addressed the commission to mark his departure, citing 'circumstances beyond our control' requiring him to leave. He praised the commission's culture of hiring for character, commended department leadership, and expressed confidence in newly appointed commissioners. The chair noted Garver was recently inducted into the Army Sports Hall of Fame in September for his hockey career at West Point, where he holds the program's all-time wins record with 75 victories.

With Garver's departure creating a vacancy in the vice president role, Commissioner Lisa nominated Veta Perkins (referred to as 'V') for vice president. Another commissioner moved to close nominations, and the motion to elect Perkins as VP passed unanimously. The chair also appointed Lisa as commission secretary without a formal vote, stating it was an appointment rather than an election.
The chair asked for corrections to the August 24 minutes. None were raised. A motion to approve was made and seconded, passing unanimously with no discussion.

Fire Deputy Chief Justin reported nine new apprentices starting that day from a pool of 45 applicants, calling the field strong. He noted six current vacancies in the department; seven candidates were interviewed for firefighter-paramedic positions but only two will advance to the PFC for approval, leaving four vacancies remaining. He also highlighted new scheduling software intended to reduce administrative burden on battalion chiefs and reduce mandatory overtime, new training software in development, a successful DEA audit of the department's controlled substances practices led by Division Chief Matt Tormolan, and the widely publicized rescue of two occupants of a small aircraft that made an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau after dark, one of whom was later identified as a gubernatorial candidate.

Chief Barnes reported that a recent police hiring process drew 40 applicants after targeted social media advertising in Wisconsin, and described the preliminary interview pool as the best the department has seen. He said the department anticipates hiring eight or nine officers in the next 12 months due to three current openings and five or six expected retirements. On budget, Barnes said the department is leaving two positions unfilled through August to meet required savings, and that the overall authorized FTE count is dropping from 81 to 80 in 2027 as foundation funding for one of two downtown homeless outreach officer positions expires — the city will fund one position and the other will simply not be backfilled. Barnes also updated the commission on the city's proposal to acquire the UW-Wausau campus, noting the city is seeking six months for due diligence and has requested a $50,000 budget modification for expert consultants; a first council vote failed due to lack of quorum and one abstention, but the finance committee has since approved the modification and it will return to the full council. Barnes addressed the Flock license plate recognition camera system, stating the department owns 20 cameras at $50,000 per year on a five-year contract, that Flock does not sell city data, and that data is deleted after 30 days; a formal presentation to the PFC is planned for October or November.

Chief Barnes outlined the timeline for selecting a new deputy chief: letters of interest and resumes were due October 2nd, officer listening sessions with the commission (without Barnes or Fire Chief Todd present) are planned for mid-October, candidate written assignments and interviews with Barnes are set for November 11th, and PFC interviews and a vote are planned for mid-to-late November with a January 17th promotional date. Commissioners discussed whether the PFC interviews could be held during the regular November 23rd meeting; Barnes said it was feasible but noted interviews could take several hours and might require a reduced agenda.

overview: The Wausau Finance Committee met on September 22, 2026, and took action on several significant items including approving a budget modification for the 700 Grand Avenue apartment development (2-1), recommending the city fully fund lead service line replacements for the remainder of the program, and advancing a feasibility study for converting the W. Stevens Point campus into a public safety building. The committee also tabled a proposed increase to dog and cat licensing fees pending more information from Marathon County, and voted to enter closed session to discuss a potential purchase of county highway department property.

discussions.body: Jamie Hoover, 4023 Brierwood, Wausau, addressed the committee opposing the proposed increase to dog and cat license fees. Hoover argued the 66.67% proposed increase for spayed/neutered animals was excessive, compared Wausau's proposed $25 fee unfavorably to larger cities like Appleton ($6), Milwaukee ($12), and Oshkosh ($5), and noted Marathon County does not charge for cat licenses while Wausau does. Hoover also raised broader concerns about cumulative fee increases on residents including the wheel tax, water costs, and storm water fees, and warned that higher fees would discourage licensing compliance.

discussions.item: 700 Grand Avenue Development Agreement and Tax Increment Grant — Multi-Year Budget Modification
discussions.body: Patrick presented the budget modification for the apartment project at Grand Avenue and Thomas Street, noting the project was nearing completion ahead of the anticipated December 31, 2026 deadline, with certificate of occupancy expected the same day or next. Alder Tierney objected to approving the budget modification before final paperwork and invoices were in hand, comparing it to closing on a house without documents, and suggested waiting two weeks. Staff clarified the action was only a budget modification — not authorizing a payment — and that the city would not cut a check until all compliance documentation was verified. Tierney maintained her objection; the motion passed 2-1 with Tierney opposed.

discussions.item: Budget Amendment for W. Stevens Point Campus — Public Safety Building Feasibility Study
discussions.body: Chief Barnes presented a $50,000 budget amendment for feasibility studies to evaluate converting the W. Stevens Point campus into a combined police and fire public safety facility. He explained the item had previously failed at Common Council 6-1 with one abstention and three absences, in part because a member's abstention functionally counted as a no with only eight members present. Barnes noted the city's proposal to Marathon County for the RFP process was generating interest, with meetings held with County Administrator Lance Leonard, and that the $50,000 would cover architectural and engineering studies, including quotes of $25,000 from FJMA Architects and $15,000 from Five Bugles. Alder Watson expressed support for proceeding with due diligence, and the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Lead Service Line Replacement — Options for Private-Side Costs
discussions.body: Community Infrastructure Partners (CIP) presented a detailed financial overview showing Wausau has replaced over 3,500 lead service lines and is the top per-capita replacer in the nation. Presenters warned that construction costs have risen 56% over two years and recommended completing the remaining 2,800–2,900 lines by 2028 to lock in quarter-percent interest loans and principal forgiveness grants, potentially saving $17–$37 million versus waiting until the 2037 EPA deadline. Three options were presented: Option A (city covers to 75% of cost, homeowners pay gap), Option B (flat $1,000 homeowner charge), and Option C (city covers all). Alder Watson moved for Option C — city covers full cost for the remainder of the program — citing equity concerns and the low interest rate available. Alder Tierney agreed, noting it was unfair to charge residents based on neighborhood. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Procurement Policy Amendment — Suspension and Debarment Verification
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne explained that the city received audit findings in 2023 and 2024 for failing to properly document suspension and debarment checks required for federal grants. The issue stemmed from inconsistent processes and staff turnover, particularly at Metro Ride transit. No vendors were actually found to be debarred — the finding was procedural. The proposed policy amendment adds mandatory documentation steps, with additional technology fixes planned including a Workday workflow prompt and a SAM.gov API integration to auto-check vendors before payment. The committee approved the amendment unanimously with no significant debate.
This was a housekeeping item to update the resolution by removing former City Clerk Caitlyn and adding new City Clerk Rachel. The motion was approved unanimously without discussion.

discussions.item: Dog and Cat License Fee Increases
discussions.body: Staff proposed restoring the original 2026 fee increase proposal — raising the spayed/neutered dog/cat fee from $23 to $30 and reducing the microchip discount from $8 to $5, for a net fee of $25 — after the council had amended it last year. Chief Barnes explained the animal control fund has never been self-sustaining, with the cat contract with the Marathon County Humane Society costing $37,000 in 2025. Alder Tierney said she could not support such a large jump and suggested a $2–$3 increase instead. Alder Watson questioned whether Marathon County had yet set its own fees for the coming year, noting the city's action could be premature; staff confirmed they had not yet heard from the county. The committee agreed by consensus to postpone the item to the next meeting pending confirmation of Marathon County's fee schedule.

discussions.body: The committee briefly acknowledged this item in open session before moving to close session, as the real estate negotiation required confidential deliberation under Wisconsin State Statute 19.85(1)(e). A roll call vote was taken to enter closed session; all three members voted in favor. The chair indicated it was unlikely the committee would reconvene in open session to take action that evening.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Green Tree Subdivision and Marathon County Facility
discussions.body: Two residents spoke during public comment. Guy Fridtelt of 2240 Ruby Drive argued that the proposed Green Tree subdivision is in a strategic location within the village's sewer service area and that approving private wells and septics there could block future municipal sewer and water extension to the east and south, citing the village's own comprehensive plan maps. He asked the commission to consult a civil engineer before proceeding. Bernie Kramer of 2150 East State Highway 153 expressed broader frustration with village leadership and economic development decisions, including the Marathon County Highway Department facility, calling it a 'total misfit' and criticizing a lack of accountability in local government. An email from Ken Charnusky was also entered into the record.

Community Development Director Nathan [last name not stated] highlighted a Zoning Board of Appeals training opportunity in Wood County on October 13th and asked commissioners to respond by the following week if interested. He noted economic development prospects in the pipeline and emphasized the importance of clearing current old business items to allow staff capacity to address new applications. He also previewed that a short-term rental industry representative may be invited to a future meeting.

discussions.item: New Business Item D: Certified Survey Map – 2172 Wood Road / 2208 Tracy Court
discussions.body: The director described the request as a straightforward lot line adjustment between two parcels that would grant one parcel creek access it currently lacks. He noted both landowners were aware of and involved in the application and recommended approval, adding he brought it before the commission out of caution given the resulting parcel shape. Trustee Stowell (Jessica) moved to approve and Bruce Sinkula seconded; the motion was approved 5-0.

discussions.item: Old Business Item E: Conditional Use Permit – Marathon County Highway Department Garage
discussions.body: The chair noted the commission had resolved most issues at a prior meeting approximately a week and a half earlier and was down to one remaining issue: an agreement between Marathon County and Saint Ries Parish on seven listed items. The director recommended approval, noting updated findings were included in the packet and that the county should be allowed flexibility to adjust fencing following neighbor discussions. He cautioned commissioners to ensure that any referenced memo conditions were their own conditions to the applicant, not third-party agreements. Bruce Sinkula moved and Trustee Stowell seconded to approve the CUP including the seven-item agreement; the motion passed 5-0.

discussions.item: Old Business Item F: Green Tree Subdivision – Update and Possible Action
discussions.body: The director provided an update noting the application was submitted June 11 and that the developer has agreed to an extension but state law presumes approval if the village board does not act within 90 days. He reported that the two previously flagged issues — stormwater management and emergency access via Nick Avenue — have been substantially addressed: stormwater details are underway, and a gated emergency access road with a Knox box will be built by the seller north of the centerline to preserve space near an existing residence. Developer representative Jill Schofield spoke, clarifying the history of the project including a prior higher-density proposal that was rejected, the engineering study of a lift station that was deemed cost-prohibitive, and the design of the emergency access. A commissioner noted that Roth Engineering had studied a connector to Tower subdivision but found a lift station would cost close to $1 million. The director acknowledged the proposal does not fully align with the village's comprehensive plan but recommended approval under the circumstances. No formal action was taken; the matter remains with the Village Board.

discussions.item: Old Business Item G: Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Review
discussions.body: The chair and director held a wide-ranging discussion about priorities for the ordinance review. Chapter 520 (zoning) was identified as more urgent than Chapter 460. Specific issues raised included: clarity on accessory structures and sheds on vacant residential lots; storage containers; goat-raising for 4-H on residential property; accessory dwelling units (three recent inquiries noted); short-term rentals/B&Bs; and future planning for data centers and power-generating facilities. The director noted a Northland Lutheran High School concession stand septic issue has been referred to the utility committee for an ordinance change. Commissioners agreed each member would identify three items of concern within Chapter 520 to bring to the October 19th meeting, and the director suggested inviting a short-term rental industry representative to that meeting as well.

Trustees discussed e-bike and e-moto enforcement concerns, ADA intersection improvements, and the plan's role as a component of the comprehensive plan. Trustees emphasized the plan is aspirational and subject to available funding and property owner cooperation under current eminent domain law. Trustee Beck asked for medium- and long-term cost totals. Marathon County was noted to have requested a copy. The plan was approved 6-1.

discussions.body: Trustees held an extended debate over whether written comments should be read aloud at meetings, what deadlines should apply, and whether profane or derogatory content should be excluded from minutes and the public record. Village President Maloney stated he would not read letters critical of himself or the board, and preferred written comments be placed in the packet rather than read aloud. Trustee Beck argued time deadlines for submission were too restrictive and that comments received before a meeting should be distributed to the board. Trustees raised First Amendment concerns and noted that similar questions arose with the village's social media policy. The original motion by Clark was withdrawn after trustees agreed more legal research was needed on what can lawfully be excluded from the public record and what the village is legally required to do with written comments. The item was then tabled to the following month.

title: Joint Board of Trustees and Finance and HR Committee Budget Workshop
overview: The Village of Weston held a joint budget workshop between the Board of Trustees and Finance and HR Committee to review the proposed 2027 budget, covering utility funds (water, sewer, stormwater) and the general fund. Key discussions centered on Mountain Bay Metro PD budget percentage calculations, employee wage structure and market positioning, and the utility rate outlook, with trustees and staff debating how to better compensate lower-paid employees. No final budget votes were taken; decisions on wages, the pay matrix, and borrowing were deferred to the October 5th meeting.
