discussions.body: Two members of the public spoke. The first speaker, a woman identified as Grace, urged the board to think outside the box on wages, suggesting bonuses instead of across-the-board percentage raises to slow compensation growth for higher earners while accelerating pay for lower-paid employees. The second speaker, identified as living on 5000 Street Weston, raised multiple specific budget concerns: the Mountain Bay Metro PD budget showing a 3.09% increase versus the charter cap of 3% and the oversight board's approved 2.8%; the Everest Metro Municipal Court label on a $60,000 line item after that court's dissolution; a $0 allocation for building maintenance personnel despite $5,521 spent year-to-date; and criticism of the employee survey process, arguing full results were never presented to the board and that the board should set budget parameters and let department heads manage within them.

The report was acknowledged by both the Finance and HR Committee and the Board of Trustees with no significant concerns raised. Finance Director Jessica noted that aquatic expenses would not be finalized until December due to pending water utility bills. A concern was raised about refuse/recycling fuel costs trending higher, with Jessica indicating the rate may need to increase to approximately $25 and that a formula and projection would be brought back to the board in October.

Public Works Director Michael presented the water utility fund, noting Weston's water rates are on the lower end compared to neighboring communities. He reported the fund has positive net income currently, with a potential rate increase possible in the 2028-2029 timeframe if a major capital project is undertaken. Chemical costs have decreased by approximately $50,000 due to removing wells one and five from service. A spreadsheet typo was identified in the 2026 budget net assets beginning balance figure, which Jessica acknowledged needed correction. Ongoing PFAS settlement payments from 3M were confirmed as the source of miscellaneous revenue, with approximately five or six payments remaining.

Michael reported that Rim Mountain Metro Sanitary District is projecting approximately a $100,000 cost increase to Weston for 2027 due to a major wastewater treatment plant upgrade to meet phosphorus limits. He noted the sewer fund has been running at a deficit for several years, and the sale of the old sewervac truck helped close the gap in the current year, but no similar large asset exists for 2027. A sewer rate increase was identified as likely necessary in 2027. Weston's rates remain among the lower ones compared to other district partners including Kronenwetter, Rothschild, and Mosinee.

Michael described the stormwater utility, noting rates have been stable since a 2023 increase and the fund continues to show positive cash flow. A major upcoming project is the Business 51 storm pond, intended to improve compliance with DNR phosphorus requirements, with modeling showing 70-80% compliance achievement. Michael clarified that stormwater funds benefit rural areas through culvert projects, not just those with curb and gutter. Grant funding from DOT for the project and a pedestrian crossing has not yet been confirmed.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget - General Fund Revenues and Expenditures
discussions.body: Jessica presented the general fund, noting the state confirmed an allowable levy increase of $732,852 from TIF closure plus approximately $95,000 in additional operational levy capacity, for a total allowable operational levy of $6,601,041. A $54,822 decrease in the Expenditure Restraint Program aid was flagged because the village's tax rate approaching the $5 threshold resulted in a penalty-like reduction, while shared revenue increased by $52,494. The budget assumes a 3% across-the-board COLA wage increase and a 10% health insurance increase, with final health insurance figures expected September 30th. The mislabeling of the Everest Metro Municipal Court versus Rothschild Area Municipal Court was acknowledged and will be corrected.

discussions.item: Mountain Bay Metro PD Budget Percentage Debate
discussions.body: Trustees and staff engaged in extended discussion over why the Mountain Bay Metro PD budget line appeared to reflect a 3.09% increase when the charter caps increases at 3% and the oversight board approved 2.8%. Jessica explained that approximately $100,000 was moved to capital for police equipment, which skewed the percentage calculation on the remaining operating line, but the total dollar amount matched Mountain Bay's request. Trustees including Brent Olson and Barbara Ermeling expressed confusion and concern. The board directed staff to move all Mountain Bay Metro costs into the general fund operating line and shift equivalent borrowing to streets, and to reduce the capital allocation from $100,000 to $60,000 to match Mountain Bay's actual budgeted capital request, making the accounting cleaner and the percentage calculation accurate.

discussions.item: Employee Wages, Pay Matrix, and Market Positioning
discussions.body: Extensive discussion was held on employee compensation. Michael noted that 11 employees are between the midpoint and maximum of the pay matrix, and that no employee exceeds 104% of market rate. Staff and trustees discussed how annual COLA increases combined with annual matrix adjustments effectively move the finish line, making it difficult for lower-paid employees to reach the midpoint. Trustee Olson calculated that total personnel cost increases including 3% COLA, WRS, health insurance, $56,000 in public works market increases, and $15,000 in merit/market contingency totaled approximately $390,000, or roughly $9,027 per employee, prompting concern about sustainability. A trustee proposed applying a flat dollar amount rather than a flat percentage to each employee's midpoint so that lower-paid employees would receive a proportionally larger increase. Jessica and Michael agreed this concept would be brought back October 5th along with three formal motions: matrix percentage increase, salary COLA percentage, and merit/market contingency amount. Staff confirmed the $56,000 in public works market increases would be tied to GTA funds.

The board discussed results of an employee survey with a 62% participation rate (23 of 37 employees). Public comment had already raised concerns that full survey results were not presented to the board. Michael confirmed streets crews use 4-10 schedules in summer but utility staff found it logistically unworkable due to seven-day operational demands. The board reached informal consensus, with multiple trustees agreeing to discontinue considering summer hours or additional holidays and focus exclusively on financial compensation. A suggestion was made to revisit non-pay benefits on a periodic basis, perhaps every 18 months.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Hub City Wind Project
discussions.body: Ten speakers signed up, with nearly all opposing a JDA with Alliant Energy and urging the county to instead pursue intervenor status at the PSC. Speakers including Tom Wilcox of Farmland First argued a county-level JDA risks preempting township zoning authority and asked the committee to join the townships' intergovernmental committee at the PSC. Joe Kiwok of the Town of Cleveland cited Columbia County's intervention as a model to follow. Mary Clues, speaking on behalf of the Marathon County Farmers Union, urged the county to negotiate hard rather than cede its power. Dean Beck warned against signing any NDA and urged baseline road assessments before construction. discussions.body: Supervisor Mask questioned how Endrris contacted all his constituents given reports that his phone was out of service. Supervisor Robinson said regardless of authorship, the request raised real concerns but was 'overly broad' and potentially very expensive—estimating intervention costs at $50,000 to $200,000 or more depending on scope. discussions.item: Consideration of Potential Engagement with Alliant Energy – Hub City Wind Project
discussions.body: CPZ staff presented a pros/cons matrix of four options: JDA negotiation (estimated up to $20,000), PSC intervention ($50,000–$200,000), moratorium (viewed as legally unenforceable for a 100+ MW project under Wis. Stat. 66.0401), and post-CPCN appeal. Staff noted the PSC could not recall any case where intervention stopped a wind project. Supervisor Robinson moved the 'Robinson resolution,' which directs Alliant Energy to submit a proposed agreement addressing work group concerns by November 1, 2025, with a further amendment added requiring the agreement be shared with governing bodies of affected townships upon receipt. Supervisor Gao proposed an alternative amendment drawing on the second resolution (putting negotiations on hold) but it was ruled out of order as it did not amend the Robinson resolution. Corporation Counsel clarified the committee's task was simply to forward a resolution to the full County Board, not to finalize county policy. The amendment to share the agreement with townships passed with one or more opposed; the full amended resolution passed 8-2 on a roll call vote.

Administrator Leonard summarized the history: a 2021 $25 million conduit financing for Bug Tussle Wireless to build a fiber ring around Marathon County, followed by a county-approved $8 million loan ($5M to complete the ring, $3M as match for a PSC broadband grant). The ring was never completed—only half was built due to cost overruns—and Bug Tussle has now requested an additional approximately $45 million from Marathon County as part of a $500 million ask across all participating counties for BEAD projects. Infrastructure committee received the Bug Tussle presentation September 3rd. The item was moved to closed session due to bargaining considerations and potential litigation.

overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors met on September 17th and took action on multiple agenda items, most notably approving an amendment to Chapter 11.02 of the county's General Code of Ordinances updating the animal waste management ordinance after an extensive 18-month collaborative process with farmers and conservation groups. The board also approved numerous rezoning ordinances and postponed a vote on an infrastructure committee appointment after a supervisor raised concerns that the previous month's 'no' votes were based on 'sour grapes' rather than qualifications.

discussions.body: Seven of eight public speakers addressed the proposed animal waste ordinance amendment. Dairy farmers Kevin Schmiky (River Run Dairy, ~90 cows), Andrew Belter (~250 cows), Shannon Niclay (~300 cows, 2,100 acres), and Patrick Suchka (~400 acres) all expressed support, citing the value of nutrient management plans for farm finances and water quality. Michael Toris of the River Alliance of Wisconsin praised Marathon County as a statewide leader in collaborative watershed work. Tom Mueller of Miltrim Farms (~3,000 cows) supported the ordinance while stating it 'does not go far enough.' James Yetus spoke in opposition, calling the ordinance 'government overreach' and arguing that his 135-year farm operation should not be forced to adopt a nutrient management plan, and that the work group was stacked with supporters.

discussions.item: Public Comment: Town of Green Valley Rezoning
discussions.body: Mitch Maguire, speaking on behalf of the Town of Green Valley town board, argued that the board formally disapproved a rezoning of a parcel from urban agricultural zoning, that the county board must honor the town's statutory authority, and that the half-acre parcel was commercially used by a shoreline protection contractor (Lakeside Rip) and should be zoned commercial, not agricultural. Neighbor Rosley Maguire raised concerns about precedent, saying other residents had already expressed intent to rezone their own half-acre lots for storage if the petitioner's request was approved.

Supervisor Sybert addressed the item, reporting that after the previous month's 19-vote 'no' result, he called 15 of those 19 supervisors and 'not one of those 15 could say he wasn't qualified,' characterizing the opposition as 'sour grapes.' Sybert moved to postpone the vote until next month so supervisors could better evaluate the candidates. Supervisor Straw asked whether the infrastructure committee could function without a chair, and was told the vice chair would serve as acting chair and the committee could appoint an acting chair under Robert's Rules. The motion to postpone passed.

discussions.item: Town of Green Valley Sawyer Daget Rezoning (Ordinance 33-26, Item E16)
discussions.body: County land resources manager Shad Harvey explained that the 27-acre parcel is split-zoned and adjacent to general agricultural land, and that staff recommended rezoning to general agriculture to allow the property owner to build a large structure to store commercial equipment. Harvey clarified that the parcel is not a half-acre — it is 27 acres — and that the town's formal disapproval resolution did not meet statutory certification requirements. ERC voted unanimously to approve. Supervisor Ritter noted ERC considered sending it back to the town but both the petitioner and town representatives wanted a decision at the committee meeting. Supervisor Straw said he would vote against it out of deference to the town's position. Supervisor Morash noted that delay would leave the owner's equipment exposed outdoors over winter. The board approved the rezoning on a non-unanimous vote.

discussions.item: Animal Waste Ordinance Amendment (Chapter 11.02, Ordinance 41-26, Item E24)
discussions.body: County conservationist Kirsty Hidenrike and conservation analyst Matt Repang presented the ordinance, which was also reviewed by outside attorney Jane Landredy of Stafford Rosenbaum. Hidenrike described an 18-month process involving six public open houses, 13 ERC meetings, six farmer workgroup sessions, and 2,500 mailed notices. The ordinance targets winter spreading of liquid manure on frozen soils in February and March, requires nutrient management plans for relevant operations, and includes phased implementation timelines and emergency spreading provisions. Supervisor Sundowski asked detailed questions about which farms are covered, what monitoring is planned, and whether storm water from cities also contributes to algae blooms. Supervisor Morash raised concern about approving the ordinance without knowing the fee amount; Hidenrike explained that fees only apply to farms that winter-spread liquid manure and refuse to obtain a nutrient management plan, and that fee amounts would go through ERC and the county board before the 2028 implementation deadline. The amendment was approved.

discussions.item: DC Everest School District Facility Study (Educational Presentation)
discussions.body: DC Everest Superintendent Dr. Casey Nye and Director of Buildings and Grounds Jason Jablonski presented a two-year facility study driven by declining enrollment and an aging 75-year-old junior high building. The proposal involves decommissioning the junior high, redistributing grades to existing buildings, adding bus drop-off improvements at Mountain Bay Middle School, and adding a wing at the senior high. Enrollment has dropped from approximately 6,000 to 5,700 students with incoming classes of 300-350 versus graduating classes of 450. Dr. Nye said the projects could be completed with no additional tax impact if a pool renovation is excluded. Board Chair Gibbs asked about long-term enrollment trajectory. Nye noted a junior high walkthrough is scheduled for October 6th for interested supervisors.

publicComment: Eight speakers signed up for public comment. Seven spoke on the animal waste ordinance: dairy farmers Kevin Schmiky, Andrew Belter, Shannon Niclay, and Patrick Suchka all expressed support, citing the collaborative process and financial and environmental benefits of nutrient management plans. Michael Toris of the River Alliance of Wisconsin praised Marathon County's watershed collaboration. Tom Mueller of Miltrim Farms (3,000 cows) supported the ordinance but said it did not go far enough. James Yetus of the town of Easton spoke in opposition, calling it government overreach and arguing the workgroup was not representative of opponents. Two speakers — Mitch Maguire and Rosley Maguire — spoke on the Town of Green Valley rezoning, urging the board to honor the town's formal disapproval and warning of precedent-setting risk if agricultural zoning is applied to a commercial contractor's parcel.

discussions.item: WASB Legislative Update and Statewide Referendum Landscape
discussions.body: Grabko reported that the WASB September update noted 71 Wisconsin school districts will have 78 referendum questions on the November ballot, bringing the 2026 statewide total to 154 questions across 145 districts — down from a record 241 in 2024. She noted this context was relevant given DC Everest's ongoing facility study and community survey. WASB's four legislative priorities for the 2027-29 budget cycle were also outlined, including increasing special education categorical aid and providing inflationary increases to spendable resources.

New student council president Bin Campman, a senior at DC Everest Senior High, reported on the school year's start including a sophomore orientation assembly, homecoming plans with a board games theme, and strong athletic results. Notable highlights included the girls tennis team's 14-3 record and a 5-0 sweep, boys soccer wins including a 'Derby' rivalry victory over Wausau West, and the first-ever inclusion of freshmen in homecoming activities such as powderpuff and hallway decorating.

Superintendent Dr. Nye discussed several topics: implementation of Wisconsin Act 89 tightening adult-student communication expectations; DC Everest's participation in the national Brightspots cohort with a site visit to Rothschild Elementary highlighted; launch of the community-wide facility survey running through October 9th; GTCC being fully booked every weekend for the coming year with the World Horseshoe Tournament generating an estimated $5.1 million total economic impact this summer; and a potential social media class action lawsuit that the district has been invited to join, which Nye said would be discussed in closed session next month. He also announced Rachel Rentmester as the incoming executive assistant, succeeding the retiring Ellen.

Dr. Lindell presented plans to relocate both alternative schools from their current shared building, citing declining enrollment creating feasibility for decommissioning the facility. IDEA, which transitioned from a charter school to a district program in April, is planned to move to the high school campus footprint for the next school year, enabling students greater access to senior high courses. Odyssey is planned to relocate to the 'blue wing' of Evergreen Elementary, with a separate entrance maintained. Board members asked about parent concerns; Lindell and Dr. Nye acknowledged difficult community conversations, noting parents are particularly concerned about the loss of dedicated square footage, and that fundraising suggestions were raised but cannot resolve the underlying staffing cost issues from declining enrollment. Current enrollment caps are 72 students per school; IDEA is in the upper 60s and Odyssey is also in the upper 60s.

Principal Mr. Alexen presented the completed Rothschild Raptor mural installed in August on the school's gymnasium stage. The project was funded through community partnerships including People's State Bank, the DC Everest Foundation, Clover Belt Credit Union, Brokaw Credit Union, and others. The mural features a raptor alongside imagery of Rib Mountain, Lake Wausau, and the local landscape, and was designed by local muralist Jessica Copeki. Alexen noted the school's theme this year is 'Raptor Nation.'

discussions.item: Health Insurance Renewal - Aspirus Health Plan
discussions.body: Dr. Nye presented the recommended renewal with Aspirus Health Plan for the 2027 plan year, noting an initial proposed increase of 44% was negotiated down to 31% and ultimately to 19.1% with plan design changes including increased deductibles and co-insurance. The district will maintain a 0% premium option for full-time employees, add employer HSA contributions of $1,000 single/$2,000 family, and cap part-time employee premium contributions at 30% for family coverage. Nye estimated approximately 75% of staff would not see an increase in out-of-pocket costs based on historical claims. The board approved the renewal without discussion.

HR Director Sarah presented the hiring report, noting 28 teacher hires this year consistent with 29 last year, with 71% having five or fewer years of experience and 40% previously connected to DC Everest. The teacher candidate pool has rebounded to pre-COVID levels. Support staff openings dropped from 17 to 11 since the report was compiled. Board members including Yee Leng Xiong, Larry Schaefer, and Lindsey Lewitzke asked about geographic origins of hires, retention of early-career teachers, and what board policies contribute to successful hiring. Schaefer raised concerns about the well-documented pattern of losing teachers with under five years of experience. Special education was identified as the greatest area of ongoing hiring need.

Dr. Lindell reported over 2,100 hours of professional development completed over the summer, with a focus on PLC work, academic clarity, and responsive classroom training. Over 50 staff attended responsive classroom training funded by grants, with Rothschild Elementary serving as the pilot school. Lindell noted teachers are reporting this as among the best starts to a school year they can remember, with staff physically tired but not emotionally depleted — a meaningful shift in teacher experience.

discussions.body: Bernie Kramer of 2150 East State Highway 153 addressed the committee, raising concerns about traffic management on Old Highway 51, arguing it is Kronenwetter's responsibility to coordinate with the county on traffic improvements rather than remaining passive. He also expressed skepticism about 10-year planning given how frequently elected boards change. An unidentified trustee noted she had spoken with Kramer earlier and agreed his suggestion about a potential turning lane for heavy equipment was worth considering.

discussions.item: Finance Director Report - Staffing and Operational Concerns
discussions.body: Finance Director John Jacobs provided an extensive update covering the financial audit (targeting mid-October), TID 3 closure audit (joint review board planned for November), property reassessment by Associated Appraisal (fieldwork underway on 3,000 parcels with buildings and 4,400 land parcels), and a potential future RFP for auditing services. Village Administrator Jim [last name inaudible] and Jacobs both emphasized the village is severely understaffed, with Jacobs noting there were days he was the only person in the office. Discussion centered on the need for a deputy finance director and the strain on interim clerk Kim, who is also managing election duties.

Jacobs presented a handout analyzing the impact of diesel fuel prices exceeding $4 per gallon — the threshold triggering a fuel surcharge clause in the Harter's garbage contract. Since March 2026, diesel has exceeded $4 (reaching over $6 per gallon), creating approximately $54,000 in unplanned costs for 2026, which the village plans to absorb using the $60,000 contingency reserve and $43,000 from TID 3 closure revenue. For the 2027 budget, trustees discussed three diesel price scenarios ($5.75, $6.00, $6.25 per gallon) that would add $28–$30 per household to garbage charges on top of the contract's standard 4% increase. Trustees agreed to plan for the worst-case $6.25 scenario, adding approximately $30 to the rate.

Jacobs and the administrator outlined anticipated 2027 budget additions: a deputy clerk position (funded 100% by general fund), a possible fourth utility crew member (funded by water/sewer rates), and retention of funding for the planning tech position. Police officers union contract negotiations are ongoing for a proposed three-year contract; a first bargaining session with the teamsters is scheduled for September 24. The state-mandated levy limit increase for 2027 is only $16,306, well short of anticipated cost increases, meaning the village will again need to use the general obligation debt service exception — similar to the $874,000 exception used in 2026.

Jacobs detailed a proposed restructuring of $863,200 in unspent TID 2 borrowing proceeds that cannot be used for TID 2 projects (the Flannery Jamrose project was scrapped after bids came in over $1.2 million). The funds must be spent by late 2027 and will be transferred to the village's general capital project fund, with the associated debt absorbed by the tax levy debt service fund. This eliminates one of two previously anticipated debt service 'drops' — the 2030 drop — while preserving the 2029 drop of approximately $226,000. Jacobs noted the restructuring may allow TID 2 to close a year or two earlier than scheduled. Budget workshops are scheduled for October 13 (full budget review at 5:30 p.m.), October 19 (3:00 p.m. start to accommodate Plan Commission at 6:00 p.m.), and October 20 (6:00 p.m.).

title: Town Hall Meeting: Overview of Professional City Management Models
overview: The City of Wausau held a public town hall meeting to educate residents and council members about professional city management models, specifically the city administrator and city manager forms of government. Dr. Michael Ford of UW-Oshkosh and Jay Shambo, a current interim city administrator, presented information on governance structures, fiscal data, and practical experience. No votes were taken; the meeting was informational only, though Mayor Doug Diny indicated the city is actively exploring hiring a city administrator and looking at including funding in the budget, potentially phasing in as early as mid-2027.

agenda.item: Welcome and introduction by Mayor Doug Diny
Introduction of Dr. Michael Ford and Jay Shambo

Dr. Ford: Process for changing government form under Wisconsin law

Public question and comment session

discussions.body: Dr. Ford explained that professional management refers to hiring an administrator or manager by the elected council to oversee day-to-day operations, insulating government from political volatility. He emphasized that the best form of government is the one that works for the community and is understood and accepted by residents. He stressed that role clarity is essential and that role confusion is a primary way this model fails.

discussions.item: City Manager vs. City Administrator Models
discussions.body: Dr. Ford distinguished between the Chapter 64 city manager model, used by 12 Wisconsin cities, and the more common ordinance-based city administrator model used by 117 cities. Key differences include that under the city manager model police and fire report to the manager, while under the administrator model the mayor retains that authority. Mayor Diny noted Wausau has a robust police and fire commission and a long tradition of separation, suggesting the administrator model is more appropriate.

Dr. Ford reported that 129 of 190 Wisconsin cities have an administrator or manager, making it the dominant form. Of Wausau's peer second-class cities, 10 of 15 have an administrator or manager. Fiscal data from the Wisconsin Department of Revenue showed professionally managed cities have lower general government operational spending per capita but slightly higher overall tax burden per capita. Jay Shambo argued a single $2 million grant could offset 10 years of administrator salary costs.

Dr. Ford addressed whether the model is anti-democratic, acknowledging that residents cannot directly vote out an administrator but retain accountability through the council. Survey data was presented showing council members under administrator forms report better group dynamics, stronger strategic planning, and clearer performance measures. Jay Shambo and a former fire chief who worked in Wausau both spoke strongly in favor of the model, with the former fire chief stating the strong mayor form is 'really inefficient' from his experience working in Wausau starting in 2000.

Dr. Ford outlined the statutory options: a two-thirds council vote to modify the charter ordinance, with a 60-day public petition window to force a referendum; a direct council vote to go to referendum; a community petition drive; or a simple ordinance change not requiring two-thirds. He cautioned against the simple ordinance route for reasons of public legitimacy and hiring attractiveness. He noted a non-binding referendum is no longer permitted under current state law.

Mayor Diny stated he has attempted to advance this idea previously, including trying to insert it into the budget, but it did not gain council traction. He indicated the city is looking at including administrator funding in an upcoming budget, possibly phasing in starting July of a future year to put half the cost in the 2027 budget. He acknowledged only one of 11 council members, Bruce Trueblood, was present at the town hall.

discussions.item: Public Comment on Council Dysfunction and Control
discussions.body: Multiple residents expressed support for the administrator model. A former council member who served 1998-2006 described budget meetings as inefficient and said an administrator would have greatly helped. Alderperson Bruce Trueblood asked attendees not to assign negative motives to absent council members, noting several were working or dealing with family emergencies. One resident raised concerns about retaining democratic control and keeping taxes manageable. A resident asked about the audit process and noted a 2021 motorpool audit whose recommendations were not fully followed.

publicComment: Numerous residents spoke from the podium. A man asked about severance costs for administrators (answered: typically 4-9 months salary, average 6 months, with no payment for cause). A resident identified as 'Ken' asked about the difference between city manager and administrator models. A woman expressed concern about retaining democratic control and the importance of elections. A former fire chief and Wausau employee from 2000 spoke at length endorsing the administrator model based on personal experience. Alderperson Bruce Trueblood defended absent council members. A long-time resident raised concerns about a 'headstrong council.' A former council member named Christine praised the administrator model's efficiency benefits. A man named David asked about why Stevens Point declined to adopt the model and whether any city has reversed course. A resident asked how the decision would be made - council or voters. A reporter identified as BC Kowalski from the Wasonian asked the mayor why this is coming up now. Eric Fonce from the Wausau Daily Herald asked about staggering alderperson terms. Additional residents asked about debt management, protected employee classes, and administrator contract structures.

discussions.body: The board voted to approve the list of law firms the district and board may access for legal services as deemed necessary by the superintendent or designee. President Bouché noted that a summary report of all 2025-26 legal council expenses had been presented by Assistant Superintendent of Operations Dr. Elizabeth Channel at the August Committee of the Whole meeting and required no separate action. The motion to approve the firm list passed.

The board approved Monday, September 28, 2026 as the date for the 2026-27 annual meeting and budget hearing, to be held at 5:00 p.m. in the Nicholson Boardroom at the Longfellow Administration Center. The budget hearing will precede the annual meeting, consistent with statutory requirements under Wis. Stat. 120.081A.

The board approved a preliminary 2026-27 general fund budget of $118,037,018 (as stated verbally, though the exact figure was slightly garbled in the transcript) for both expenses and revenue for presentation at the annual meeting and budget hearing. Property values in the district are projected to increase 4.03% for mill rate calculation purposes, with certified values not available until October 1.
The board approved a projected tax levy of $45,848,693 for presentation at the annual meeting and budget hearing. No discussion was recorded before the vote.

A presenter (name not clearly identified in transcript) reported that 30 students districtwide required seclusion or restraint interventions in 2025-26, up from 22 the prior year, with a combined total of 34 incidents (six seclusions, 24 restraints, four combined). Board Member Pat McKee asked how often classrooms are evacuated due to a single student's behavior and whether that data is tracked; the presenter noted such evacuations would not be counted as seclusion or restraint unless the student was physically confined. Board Member Jennifer Paoli asked for clarification on the definitions of seclusion and restraint. The board voted to approve the report as presented.

discussions.item: Board Member Reports and Superintendent Update
discussions.body: Board Member Cory Sillars highlighted the Build My Future event on September 23 at KBY Window and Door, open houses at Rib Mountain, Franklin, and Jimmy Jones schools, and raised legislative concerns about potential impacts if Act 10 is repealed or if DPI undergoes leadership changes after the upcoming election. Superintendent Bushman reported nine days of school completed, acknowledged early-year HVAC issues at Marshall and Franklin schools, praised the Wausau West community for managing traffic congestion, and recognized First Student bus manager Dennis Gart for improved busing operations. President Bouché noted upcoming WIAA regional meeting at Antigo on September 17 and WASB Region 5 annual meeting in Wausau/Rothschild on September 29.
The board voted unanimously via roll call to enter closed session for preliminary discussion regarding potential litigation under Wisconsin Statute 19.85(g). All eight members present voted yes.

publicComment: One speaker identified as Jeff addressed the board, alleging that district administrators at Horace Mann Middle School lied to police and the community following an incident captured on video, and that the board spent nearly $100,000 in legal fees — including approximately $20,000 paid to his attorney — to resist open records requests related to the matter. He called on the board to hold the superintendent and an unnamed vice principal accountable and characterized the board as unwilling to exercise independent oversight.

title: Plan Commission
overview: The Village of Weston Plan Commission held its September 14, 2026 meeting, addressing three conditional use permit compliance cases involving USM Storage (3107 Concord Ave), Bug Properties (6406 Schofield Ave), and Tommy's Car Wash (1611 Schofield Ave), as well as approving two subdivision/plat items. The commission voted to initiate modification proceedings for USM Storage's CUP due to ambiguity in the approved site plan, found Bug Properties in non-compliance and set a September 23 deadline before a public hearing, and found Tommy's Car Wash out of compliance for failing to provide five years of required inspection reports and insurance certificates, also setting a September 23 deadline.

discussions.body: Jim Pinsol (address not stated) submitted a written public comment read into the record criticizing inconsistencies in how staff handled the three CUP violation cases, alleging bias, lack of accountability, missing timelines, and gross negligence regarding Tommy's Car Wash being in a wellhead protection area for five years without required documentation. He also called on any commissioner with financial ties to affected properties to recuse themselves. Online commenter Jake (last name not stated), owner of townhomes at 314/318 Ross Avenue, read a letter detailing his concerns about USM Storage expanding gravel and RV parking into green space beyond permit boundaries, water runoff erosion on his property, and the precedent set by owner Mr. Minell repeatedly making unpermitted improvements.

Staff presented a preliminary/final condominium plat for 4603-4613 Camp Phillips Road, where Lockree Development is purchasing the Vendor family property to establish a four-unit condominium plat. A representative from Lockree Development explained the road and stormwater pond would be common elements and the arrangement would function similarly to the existing rental use. Staff reported no revisions needed and recommended approval subject to eight conditions. The commission approved the plat unanimously.

discussions.item: Amended Final Plat - Bold Junior View Subdivision (Project 20250424)
discussions.body: Staff explained the original final plat approved in July 2026 was never recorded, and the Wisconsin DNR subsequently required a 60-foot public access easement to Bull Junior Creek affecting lots 12 and 13, making them slightly smaller. Since the plat was unrecorded, the developer amended it to incorporate the easement and returned for reapproval. One commissioner asked whether all six conditions in the packet should be included; staff clarified they would all appear on the village board resolution, with condition four (public access easement) being the only new addition. The commission approved the amended plat unanimously.

discussions.item: CUP Compliance - USM LLC, 3107 Concord Avenue
discussions.body: Staff reported USM Storage was parking RVs and trailers in a designated green space and had added gravel, expanding beyond what the approved site plan showed. Property owner Steve Minell argued the site was in compliance with the April 2024 CUP approval, stating vehicles in the green space had been moved by August 19-20 and that gravel maintenance was not new expansion. Online neighbor Jake disputed this, stating new gravel extended roughly 12 feet into the green space. Commission members debated at length that the approved site plan lacked dimensional specifications for the green space buffer, making enforcement subjective. Ultimately the commission agreed a modification was needed to establish a clear numerical setback, and voted to direct staff to commence modification proceedings and schedule a public hearing rather than finding the owner definitively non-compliant.

discussions.item: CUP Compliance - Bug Properties, 6406 Schofield Avenue
discussions.body: Staff presented detailed findings showing the property at 6406 Schofield Avenue had not been completed per the approved site plan, with a CUP completion deadline of October 9, 2025 having passed nearly a year prior. Outstanding items included concrete work, fencing, gates, landscaping, and curbing; the building permit had also expired. Staff reported owner Bruce Gus had not responded to emails or phone calls, with his voicemail box full. Commissioners expressed frustration at the lack of response and agreed the September 23, 2026 compliance deadline in the motion was generous. The commission voted to find the property non-compliant and set a September 23 deadline, directing staff to schedule a public hearing at the October 12 plan commission meeting if not resolved.

discussions.item: CUP Compliance - Tommy's Car Wash, 1611 Schofield Avenue
discussions.body: Staff reported that Tommy's Car Wash had failed to provide required annual underground sediment tank inspection reports and a certificate of environmental insurance for multiple consecutive years, with only a 2021 report on file. Staff noted the facility is located in a wellhead protection area and that outreach since January 2026 had yielded no documentation and no response. Commissioners expressed strong concern about the wellhead protection implications, with one member arguing this case warranted more urgency than a green space dispute. The commission voted to find the CUP out of compliance and directed staff to send written notice with a September 23, 2026 deadline, with the matter returning to the commission for further action if not resolved.

Jake (online, owner of townhomes at 314/318 Ross Avenue) read a letter expressing concerns about USM Storage owner Minell repeatedly expanding gravel and RV parking into green space beyond his permit, causing water runoff erosion on Jake's property, and asking the commission to require reversion to permit compliance.

discussions.body: Alan Wussellowski, city engineer with 26 years of service, addressed the committees expressing concern that the family deductible increase from $3,400 to $6,000 represents a roughly $3,000 per year additional burden on employees and warned it would hinder recruitment, citing a city surveyor position that has gone unfilled for two years with no applicants. HR Director Keenan responded that the city went to market and the Aspirus plan was the best available, noting the original premium increase proposed was 20.3% and was negotiated down to 9.6% in part through the deductible increases; she also noted the county's deductibles are higher ($4,000 single / $6,500 family) and city employees pay only 12% of premiums versus the county's 15%. Alder Hickeyi raised that the deductible increase for families represents roughly a 76% increase and questioned whether the city could increase HSA contributions, to which staff indicated that adding $600 per family plan would cost approximately $101,400 more on top of the already $550,000 premium increase, totaling over $650,000 in additional budget exposure. Keenan noted that 75% of employees with health insurance do not currently reach the maximum out-of-pocket and that the city also provides a 3% COLA plus merit increases, which is better than many employers.

title: Plan Commission Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Plan Commission held a special September 10, 2026 meeting focused primarily on a conditional use permit for a Marathon County Highway Facility proposed at 2384-2388 Old Highway 51. The meeting drew significant public comment raising concerns about coal dust health hazards, road maintenance responsibility, tax revenue loss, and cemetery compatibility. The commission did not take a final vote, instead discussing conditions and leaning toward postponing a decision to its September 21 meeting to allow time for a written agreement between the county and St. Therese Gate of Heaven Cemetery and to resolve outstanding issues around road cost-sharing and zoning ordinance completion.

discussions.item: Conditional Use Permit - Marathon County Highway Facility (Public Hearing)
discussions.body: Multiple public speakers addressed the commission. Joel Straub, Marathon County Supervisor for District 15, raised health and safety concerns about coal dust drift from the adjacent WPS power plant, citing state statute 709 on property condition disclosures, and urged the commission to require air quality data before approving. Speaker (identified as Mr. Baker) requested two conditions: a jurisdictional transfer of Business 51 from the village to the county for road maintenance, and widening Business 51 to four lanes from south of Village Way to the facility driveway. Kent Sharnosky argued the application failed all five conditional use criteria, challenged whether the required M2 zoning ordinance amendment had been properly completed, cited Wisconsin court cases placing the burden of proof on the applicant, and called the deal one-sided with no benefit to Kronenwetter residents. Bernie Kramer criticized the absence of village administrative leadership and echoed road upgrade concerns. Attorney Matt Edie spoke on behalf of St. Therese Gate of Heaven Cemetery, noting potential notice issues with the prior zoning change and requesting conditions to protect cemetery operations regarding noise, hours, and buffers.

discussions.item: Marathon County Response to Public Hearing Concerns
discussions.body: Marathon County Deputy Administrator Chris Holman described a hastily drafted two-page memo outlining a voluntary condition proposal to address St. Therese Cemetery concerns: a solid 8-foot fence along approximately 1,200 feet of the property line, supplemented by evergreen trees and shrubs, to be triggered when the active cemetery operations approach within 100 feet of the property line within a 12-month notice window. Highway Commissioner Kevin Lane addressed traffic concerns, stating JT Engineering analysis found no turn lanes would be required at current 5,000 vehicles/day volume on Old 51, and that the new location would have far fewer conflict points than the existing facility on 17th Avenue. Holman acknowledged coal dust concerns but stated WPS is federally and state regulated, noted a 2010 lawsuit resolved particulate emissions issues, and said they planned a higher MERV-rated HVAC filter as a proactive measure. He could not commit to jurisdictional road transfer or cost-sharing, stating those decisions require county committee and board approval.

discussions.item: Commission Discussion on Conditions and Path Forward
discussions.body: Commission members discussed the open-ended nature of unresolved conditions including the cemetery buffer agreement (not yet finalized), road maintenance cost-sharing on Old Business 51, and whether the M2 zoning ordinance change had been properly completed as required by village ordinance. Commissioner Bruce noted he wanted to see the fence/buffer agreement in writing before approving it as a condition. Trustee Lesniak summarized three key issues requiring resolution: finalization of the cemetery buffer agreement, a road cost-sharing or maintenance arrangement for Old Business 51, and confirmation the zoning change was properly codified by ordinance. The commission did not reach a vote, with members leaning toward postponing to the September 21 meeting to allow conditions to be properly documented, while county representatives requested specific direction on outstanding issues to address before that meeting.

discussions.item: Zoning Change - William Sywinsky, 1900/1904 Lea Road
discussions.body: William Sywinsky appeared and briefly explained the request to rezone 26.7 acres from Agricultural-Residential to RR-5 Rural Residential, stating the property has been in the family since 1972, his parents have passed, the family is trying to sell the home, and the rezoning is needed because the parcel is under 10 acres and they wish to adjust property lines. No other public speakers addressed this item. No vote was taken at this stage as it was the public hearing portion.

discussions.item: Text Amendment - Chapter 520 Zero Lot Line Homes
discussions.body: Bernie Kramer was the only public speaker, asking for more information on how zero lot line homes would be integrated with existing large lots in Kronenwetter, whether all homes in a new development could be zero lot line, and what the strategy would be for mixing lot sizes. No commission discussion or vote was recorded on this item beyond receiving public input.

An unidentified speaker referred to as Mr. Baker requested road jurisdictional transfer and four-lane widening of Business 51 as permit conditions. Kent Sharnosky (2604 16th Road) argued the application failed all five conditional use criteria and raised a procedural zoning ordinance deficiency.
